idiom_name: generic Seq->Seq combinator functions over iter.Seq[T] (Go 1.23) + slices/maps terminals
implementation_notes: Go 1.23's range-over-func iterators give the pattern both ends: a source is any iter.Seq[T] (slices.Values, maps.Keys/Values, a file walker, a database cursor), a terminal is slices.Collect/Sorted/Chunk or a plain for-range, and a transformation is an ordinary generic function func(iter.Seq[A]) iter.Seq[B] that the team writes - Map and Filter are five lines each because the stage is just a closure that calls yield and returns immediately when yield reports the consumer stopped. What replaces the classic structure: no reducer protocol exists in Go, and none is needed - the push iterator (yield returning bool) carries early termination, and iter.Pull converts to a pull iterator when the consumer must drive. Composability is by nesting or a small local Compose helper rather than by a library; the classic object/interface form is justified only when stages must be registered dynamically or an existing codebase already exposes hand-rolled Iterator interfaces.
pitfalls: Ignoring the boolean returned by yield keeps producing after the consumer broke out of the loop - the iterator must return immediately or the work (and any allocation) continues invisibly.
iter.Seq runs in the consumer's goroutine: a blocking stage blocks the caller, and multiple concurrent producers still need channels - iter.Seq is sequential streaming, not concurrency.
A pull iterator obtained from iter.Pull spawns a goroutine and must be released with its stop function; dropping it leaks the goroutine, and ranging a push iterator twice re-runs the body.
